notes: Second appeal on void-for-uncertainty challenge to boundary consent order; Rix LJ allowed appeal after 15 years of litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Scammell v Dicker: certainty of boundary dispute consent order
key_facts: Neighbours at Glenwood Farm and Hillside in Dorset litigated their boundary from 1989; a consent order in February 1994 fixed the line on plan D4 between points A and B along the western bank of a hedgerow.
Surveyors pegged a line on site in February 1994 but solicitors' approval was never finalised; the Scammells later sued to set aside the order for uncertainty or mistake.
HHJ Rudd declared the consent order void for uncertainty in 2002; Mr Justice McCombe dismissed appeals on uncertainty though not on costs.

The telegraph pole at the northern end showed the thick boundary line on the plan embraced an area from the hedge centre to the western bank, creating a small interpretive difficulty but not impossibility.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal on whether a February 1994 consent order settling a boundary dispute was void for uncertainty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the consent order was not void for uncertainty and the Scammells' claim to set it aside failed on its merits.
enrichment.ratio: A consent court order is not void for uncertainty merely because implementation involves interpretive difficulty or surveyor disagreement; that which can be made certain is certain, and courts should preserve rather than destroy bargains parties have acted upon.
legal_issues: Whether a consent order fixing a boundary line on a plan was void for uncertainty
Whether implementation required further agreement between the parties
Whether conflict between order text and plan rendered the settlement impossible to perform
Whether the overriding objective could bar a late challenge to a consent order
catchwords: id certum est quod certum reddi potest
linked_authorities: Mamidoil-Jetoil Greek Petroleum Co SA v Okta Crude Oil Refinery AD [2001] EWCA Civ 406

notes: Liability trial in breech caesarean birth injury case; judge rejected clotting-disorder defence and found negligence.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v Sheridan: negligent breech caesarean and neonatal brain injury
key_facts: Jake Smith was born by planned caesarean on 11 May 1999 because of breech presentation after infertility treatment.
Delivery was uncomplicated until the head became stuck; Dr Sheridan applied Wrigley forceps, widened the incision and made a documented hard pull.
Jake was born flat with Apgar scores of 0 at delivery, severe intracranial haemorrhage and ischaemic damage, and profound brain injury.

The defendant argued a pre-existing neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia clotting disorder caused bleeding; the claimant argued negligent excessive force tore cerebral veins causing haemorrhage, hypoxia and acquired DIC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues of liability and causation only in a clinical negligence claim arising from a breech caesarean delivery.
enrichment.outcome: Liability and causation found in favour of the claimant; damages assessment to follow.
enrichment.ratio: Excessive mechanical force in delivering the head during caesarean section was negligent and caused tearing of cerebral veins; the subsequent low platelet count was explained by massive bleed and acquired DIC during resuscitation rather than a pre-existing clotting disorder.
legal_issues: Whether the obstetrician breached duty in incision size and use of forceps
Whether cerebral haemorrhage was caused by negligent delivery or pre-existing NAIT
Whether low platelets at one hour indicated pre-existing clotting disorder
Causation between delivery trauma, resuscitation delay, hypoxia and brain damage

confidence.notes: Detailed liability findings on negligence and causation with explicit favourable conclusion for claimant.

notes: Police complaints dispensation judicial review; PCA failed to consider solicitor correspondence when granting dispensation.

enrichment.short_title: Clare v IPCC: quashing police complaint investigation dispensation
key_facts: Deborah Clare complained that Metropolitan Police officers used excessive force arresting her on New Year's Eve 2002, including assault and verbal abuse.

Investigation was delayed pending criminal proceedings discontinued in October 2003; Christian Khan solicitors undertook to provide a detailed statement but the investigating officer wrote directly to the complainant on 9 February 2004 threatening dispensation.
The Police Complaints Authority granted dispensation on 26 March 2004 because no statement had been received, ignoring the 23 January solicitor letter and prior complaint details.
PC John Davies, an officer subject to the complaint, opposed quashing because he had been told the matter was concluded and delay would prejudice him.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full judicial review hearing after a mistaken consent order was set aside; claim to quash PCA dispensation from investigating the complaint.
enrichment.outcome: Dispensation decision of 26 March 2004 quashed; relief refused on discretionary delay grounds; mandatory reconsideration order declined.
enrichment.ratio: A dispensation decision vitiated by failure to take account of the undertaking to send correspondence to the complainant's solicitors and active solicitor engagement must be quashed; delay did not warrant refusing relief where unlawful decision would have produced the same investigative consequences if challenged earlier.
legal_issues: Whether the PCA failed to take a material consideration when granting dispensation
Whether dispensation should be refused on discretionary grounds of delay
Whether the only reasonable outcome was dispensation given elapsed time
Standing and prejudice to PC Davies as interested party
linked_authorities: R v Police Complaints Authority ex parte Broome (unreported, 6 December 1988)
R (Wilkinson) v Police Complaints Authority [2004] EWHC 678 (Admin)

notes: Asylum appeal on internal relocation and compartmentalised credibility; IAT approach upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Solonina v SSHD: internal flight alternative and credibility compartmentalisation
key_facts: A Ukrainian Orthodox Christian claimed asylum after alleged attacks by Greek Catholics in Ivano-Frankivsk in March and October 2000 and police failure to protect him.
Adjudicator Mr Hollingworth accepted some facts but rejected credibility on core persecution claims and found internal relocation available across Ukraine.

Before the IAT both parties agreed corroborative country material showed the adjudicator inadequately dealt with core claim evidence; the IAT proceeded on the claim at its strongest on passport and relocation issues.
The IAT upheld findings that withheld passports could be replaced and that registration and modest bribery costs did not make internal relocation unduly harsh.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal on internal relocation and treatment of adverse credibility findings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no error of law in treating internal flight alternative separately or rejecting collusion argument.
enrichment.ratio: Whether Article 8 or asylum credibility issues can be compartmentalised depends on the facts; the IAT could lawfully uphold passport and internal relocation findings even where core persecution credibility was flawed, and thin evidence of police collusion did not require separate treatment.
legal_issues: Whether credibility is indivisible once a material adverse finding is flawed
Whether internal relocation analysis could proceed assuming claim at its strongest
Whether police collusion with Greek Catholics was overlooked
Application of Erdogan v SSHD on compartmentalised credibility
linked_authorities: Erdogan v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1472
CA v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1165

notes: Case stated appeal on restriction order attached to insanity Act admission; Court of Appeal allowed appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Narey v C&E: restriction order under insanity Act admission procedure

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991

key_facts: Mr Narey, aged 65, was found unfit to plead after importing 3.38 kilos of cocaine from Grenada while suffering a manic episode of bipolar disorder.
A jury found he did the act charged; Judge MacRae made a hospital admission order with an unlimited restriction direction under Schedule 1 paragraph 2(1)(b) of the 1991 Act.
Psychiatrists said he was non-compliant with medication in prison and needed hospital assessment; the judge imposed restriction without specific evidence of risk of serious harm to others.
The Secretary of State later remitted Narey for trial; he pleaded guilty and sentencing under section 37 was pending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Crown Court restriction direction attached to insanity Act admission order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; restriction direction wrongly imposed because section 41 criteria were not satisfied and no finding of risk of serious harm was made.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5 of the 1964 Act admission route is distinct from section 41 Mental Health Act procedure; while psychiatric evidence may assist, a restriction without limitation requires evidence of risk of serious harm to the public and cannot be based merely on unpredictability or concern about medication compliance.
legal_issues: Whether section 41(2) psychiatric evidence requirements apply to Schedule 1 paragraph 2(1)(b) directions
Whether drug importation constitutes serious harm for restriction purposes
Whether restriction can be imposed when court cannot be satisfied defendant would not pose serious harm
Distinction between 1964/1991 insanity procedure and section 37/41 Mental Health Act orders

notes: Case stated on whether Volvo franchise inner car park was public place for careless driving; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: May v DPP: careless driving in Volvo garage customer car park
key_facts: On 5 June 2003 the appellant's Renault collided with five parked cars in the inner car park of a Volvo franchise garage at Barkingside Motor Co on Fencepiece Road.
The inner car park was enclosed by a gate closed evenings but accessible from the main road without obstacle during opening hours, with signs inviting customer parking for sales, service and parts.
Magistrates convicted of careless driving; Snaresbrook Crown Court upheld conviction holding the car park was a public place unlike the small office yard in R v Spence.
The appellant argued business customers formed a special class and premises entered for commercial reasons were not public places under DPP v Vivier.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Crown Court dismissal of appeal against careless driving conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Question answered in the affirmative; appeal dismissed; inner car park held a public place.
enrichment.ratio: A commercial car park open to all members of the public without selective admission during business hours, adjoining a public road and inviting custom, is a public place for section 3 Road Traffic Act purposes even though users attend for business reasons.
legal_issues: Whether garage customer car park was a public place under section 3 Road Traffic Act 1988
Whether business customers cease to be members of the public
Application of DPP v Vivier and Harrison v Hill special-class analysis
Distinction from R v Spence small office yard

confidence.notes: Focused statutory construction issue with clear affirmative answer and dismissal of appeal.

notes: Transcript covers only preliminary applications before main guarantee appeal; stay and recusal refused.

enrichment.short_title: Dobbs v Triodos Bank: preliminary stay and recusal applications refused
key_facts: Mr Dobbs appealed in person against declarations made by HHJ Havelock-Allan QC in a guarantee dispute with Triodos Bank NV.
Dobbs sought a stay pending European Court of Human Rights proceedings to obtain legal aid, arguing inequality of arms against bank counsel.
He also sought general stay and recusal of Lord Justice Chadwick because Strasbourg proceedings criticised the judiciary for favouring represented litigants.
The appeal concerned declarations only, not payment orders; a related April 2002 order was the substantive guarantee enforcement subject.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing on preliminary applications before opening of appeal against guarantee declarations.
enrichment.outcome: Applications to stay proceedings and for Chadwick LJ to recuse refused; stay of execution application deferred until after judgment on merits if needed.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant in person does not automatically obtain stay for pending Strasbourg legal aid proceedings if the court can reach a just conclusion with counsel's assistance; criticism of judges in separate proceedings is not a sufficient ground for recusal without showing actual bias.
legal_issues: Whether appeal should be stayed pending ECtHR legal aid application
Whether judge should recuse for litigant's Strasbourg criticisms
Whether court could fairly determine complex guarantee appeal with unrepresented appellant
Whether stay of execution should be indicated in advance of merits decision

notes: CIS certificate renewal appeal; Commissioners wrongly applied proportionality test to late PAYE payments.

enrichment.short_title: Barnes v Hilton Main: CIS sub-contractor certificate renewal refusal
key_facts: Hilton Main Construction sought renewal of a construction industry scheme gross-payment certificate under section 565 ICTA 1988.
All 31 PAYE, NIC and CIS payments during the qualifying period were late; corporation tax was also paid late on two occasions.
General Commissioners allowed appeal citing Revenue failure to warn, wife's withdrawal of funds and risk to 51 employees' jobs, applying a proportionality test.
The company had paid no tax within the qualifying period on time; average lateness ranged from 33 to 100 days across years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from General Commissioners allowing taxpayer appeal against CIS certificate renewal refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Revenue appeal allowed; Commissioners' decision quashed; certificate should not have been issued given non-minor late payment failures.
enrichment.ratio: Section 565(4) requires both minor-and-technical character and no doubt about future compliance; late payment under section 565(8A) counts as non-compliance; Commissioners cannot apply a separate proportionality test under the Human Rights Act where the statutory scheme is Convention-compliant.
legal_issues: Whether persistent late PAYE payments were minor and technical under section 565(4)
Whether Hudson v JDC two-hurdle construction of section 565(4) applies
Whether refusal disproportionate under Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR
Whether section 3 Human Rights Act permits reading proportionality into CIS certificate scheme

notes: Patent licence clause 14.4 rectified for unilateral mistake; subject-to-contract offers insufficient.

enrichment.short_title: QRS v BTG: patent licence first-offer clause rectification and compliance
key_facts: BTG granted QRS an exclusive licence of 77 nuclear quadrupole resonance patents across multiple countries in September 2002.
Clause 14.4 as drafted only required first offer to QRS before BTG abandoned patents, not before commercial assignment to a third party.
In March 2004 BTG negotiated to sell the portfolio to InVision Technologies and made subject-to-contract offer letters to QRS on 10 March and 8/9 April 2004.
BTG's lawyer Mr Ali had told QRS solicitors the principle of a first-offer right on assignment was okay but deliberately redrafted clause 14.4 to exclude assignment scenarios.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial on construction, rectification and compliance of patent licence clause 14.4 first-offer obligation.
enrichment.outcome: Clause 14.4 rectified to apply on assignment as well as abandonment; BTG's subject-to-contract letters did not comply; injunctive relief granted substantially for QRS.
enrichment.ratio: Rectification for unilateral mistake is available where a licensor's lawyer knowingly misrepresented that a redrafted clause gave effect to an agreed first-offer principle; compliance with a first-offer clause requires a contractual offer capable of immediate acceptance, not a subject-to-contract invitation to negotiate.
legal_issues: Whether clause 14.4 triggered on proposed assignment not merely abandonment
Whether rectification for unilateral mistake by QRS should be ordered against BTG
Whether subject-to-contract offer letters satisfied first-offer obligation
Whether meeting on 16 March 2004 varied clause 14.4 or created binding agreement
linked_authorities: George Wimpey UK Limited v VI Components Limited [2005] EWCA Civ 77
Bircham & Co (Nominees) (No.2) Ltd v Worrell Holdings Limited [2001] EWCA Civ 775

confidence.notes: Comprehensive Chancery judgment resolving construction, rectification and compliance issues.

notes: Renewed permission application on third-party vandal liability; Smith v Littlewoods category three arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Davies v Stockwell: vandalised fencing and trip injury liability
key_facts: A building contractor cordoned off a demolition site in a poorly lit public precinct with metal posts and orange bunting after relaying paving stones over concrete bases.
Vandals pulled the posts causing a paving stone to stand proud; the bunting was also vandalised so the claimant tripped and broke her ankle late at night.
The trial judge held the defendant liable for leaving posts and bunting where vandals were likely to create danger, placing the case in Smith v Littlewoods third category.
The defendant argued the proud paving stone not the posts was the danger source and posts unvandalised were not dangerous.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal after refusal on paper against liability judgment of HHJ Isobel Parry.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal to be heard by three judges with half-day time limit.
enrichment.ratio: At permission stage it is arguable that liability under Smith v Littlewoods third category requires a state of danger exploited by third parties, not merely property left where known vandals may convert innocuous equipment into danger; whether leaving posts in a vandal-prone unlit area suffices remains unsettled.
legal_issues: Whether defendant was responsible for a state of danger exploited by vandals under Smith v Littlewoods
Whether proud paving stone rather than posts was the true source of danger
Whether posts and bunting left overnight were themselves dangerous
Liability for wrongful acts of third parties in construction site fencing
linked_authorities: Smith v Littlewoods Organisation Ltd [1987] AC 241

confidence.notes: Permission judgment clearly identifies arguable Smith v Littlewoods point though merits unresolved.
